Statues of Ramses the Great being reassembled after having been moved to save them from being flooded during construction of the Aswan Dam. Egypt. 1967

These statues are part of the Abu Simbel temples which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the "Nubian Monuments. The twin temples were originally carved out of the mountainside during the reign of Pharaoh Ramesses II in the 13th century BC, as a lasting monument to himself and his queen Nefertari,

The complex was relocated in its entirety to prevent them being submerged during the creation of Lake Nasser, the reservoir formed after the building of the Aswan High Dam on the Nile River.

The salvage of the temples began in 1964 by a multinational team of archeologists, engineers and skilled heavy equipment operators working together under the UNESCO banner. It cost some $40 million at the time. The entire site was carefully cut into large blocks (averaging 20 tons), dismantled, lifted and reassembled in a new location 65 meters higher and 200 meters back from the river, in one of the greatest challenges of archaeological engineering in history.
